WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate on Tuesday approved a five-year highway and transit bill that would send more than $300 billion to states for road repairs, bridge replacements and bus fleets, ending months of negotiations that at times threatened to stall federal construction money heading into the winter.

The measure passed 71-27, with a coalition of Democrats and rural Republicans overcoming objections from conservatives who said the bill spends too much and from progressive senators who wanted a larger share of the money reserved for public transit and electric vehicle charging.

Senate Majority Leader Dana Whitfield called the vote a rare moment of cooperation. "Every one of our states has a bridge that should have been fixed a decade ago," Whitfield said on the Senate floor. "Today we stopped arguing about whose fault that is."

The bill now goes to the House, where Speaker Paul Renner has said he wants changes to how money is divided between large metropolitan areas and smaller communities. Several House Republicans from farm districts have said the Senate formula shortchanges counties with long stretches of two-lane highway and few residents to pay for them.

Transportation Secretary Lena Ortiz said the administration supports the Senate version and urged the House to act before the current authorization expires at the end of the month. Without an extension, the Transportation Department would have to delay reimbursements to states for projects already under way.

The bill includes $42 billion for bridge repair, $18 billion for transit agencies and a new competitive grant program for freight corridors near ports and rail yards. It also sets aside money to replace aging culverts that flood during heavy storms, a provision pushed by senators from coastal states.

Budget analysts estimate the plan would add about $60 billion to deficits over ten years unless Congress finds new revenue, since fuel tax collections have fallen as cars become more efficient.

Associated Press writer Mark Delaney contributed to this report.
